q: בת 85 אובחנה כסובלת מ- Polymyalgia Rheumatica (PMR). מה נכון בנוגע למחלה זו?
o: התסמונת שכיחה יותר אצל נשים ביחס של 2:1
70% מחולי PMR הם בגיל מעל 60
כאבים בחגורת אגן יותר שכיחים מאשר כאבים בחגורת כתפיים
ב- 40% מהחולים יש ארטריטיס ארוזיבי של מפרקי כפות הידיים
explanation:
Official answer: א

**Polymyalgia rheumatica (PMR)** is an inflammatory syndrome of older adults with proximal muscle pain and stiffness. Its epidemiology and nonerosive inflammatory pattern explain the distinctions in these options (pp. 1600–1601).

**A. Twice as common in women as in men.** Correct, the source gives a female-to-male ratio of 2:1, matching the official answer (p. 1600).
**B. 70% of patients are older than 60.** Wrong, PMR occurs from age 50 onward, but 90% of cases occur after 60. The proposed percentage understates its concentration in the older group (p. 1600).
**C. Hip-girdle pain is more common than shoulder-girdle pain.** Wrong, shoulder pain is more frequent than hip pain, making it a particularly characteristic manifestation (p. 1601).
**D. Erosive hand arthritis occurs in 40%.** Wrong, mild symmetric arthritis of the hands, wrists and knees can occur, but it is nonerosive. The destructive component of this option does not fit PMR (p. 1601).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1600, 1601.

q: מה מהבאים נכון לגבי תופעות לואי של טיפול באופיואידים בכאב כרוני בזקנים?
o: עצירות היא תופעת לוואי שמתפתחת לה סבילות ( TOLERANCE ) עם הזמן
עקב תופעות הלוואי אסור לעבור מינון מקסימלי של אופיואידים (CEILING EFFECT)
PSEUDOADDICTION היא תופעת לוואי המתבטאת בצריכה מופרזת של תרופה משנית לגורמים לא אורגניים
בהפסקה פתאומית של הטיפול יכולים להיות סימני גמילה
explanation:
**Physical dependence is not addiction**: opioid agonists can cause withdrawal when stopped (Hazzard 8e, p. 326). Constipation needs preventive treatment and monitoring; one should not wait on the assumption that it will necessarily disappear with continued use (p. 1075).

**A. Tolerance to constipation develops with time.** Wrong, tolerance to constipating effects may never occur, so time cannot be relied on to resolve constipation. The geriatric source recommends starting laxatives with opioids (Hazzard, p. 1075; AAPM/APS/ASAM consensus, 2001, p. 3).
**B. Adverse effects impose a maximum opioid dose, a ceiling effect.** Wrong, pure opioid agonists do not share a uniform pharmacologic dose ceiling in the sense proposed; clinical escalation remains limited by safety and adverse effects. This does not authorize unlimited dosing (AAPM/APS/ASAM, p. 3).
**C. Pseudoaddiction means excessive drug use caused by nonorganic factors.** Wrong, the historical term described drug-seeking attributed to undertreated pain, not use caused by nonorganic factors. Its validity as a distinct diagnosis was not established in the literature review, so it should not justify automatic opioid escalation (Greene and Chambers, 2015, concluding discussion; AAPM/APS/ASAM, p. 3).
**D. Abrupt discontinuation can cause withdrawal.** Correct, opioid agonists can cause physical dependence, so abruptly stopping sustained treatment may cause withdrawal; withdrawal alone does not prove addiction (Hazzard, p. 326).

Eighth-edition verification: Opioid agonists can cause physical dependence and withdrawal when stopped, supporting the withdrawal option. The discussion of buprenorphine's ceiling on respiratory depression must not be generalized to a uniform dose ceiling for all opioids (Hazzard 8e, p. 326).
Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 326, 1075; AAPM/APS/ASAM. Definitions Related to the Use of Opioids for the Treatment of Pain. 2001, p. 3, https://www.naabt.org/documents/APS_consensus_document.pdf; Greene MS, Chambers RA. Pseudoaddiction: Fact or Fiction? Curr Addict Rep. 2015;2:310-317, concluding discussion, doi:10.1007/s40429-015-0074-7.

q: מה מאפיין כאב גב מותני בחולים הסובלים מהיצרות ספינאלית?
o: הכאב מחמיר במעבר משכיבה לישיבה
הכאב מחמיר בהליכה בעליה
הכאב מחמיר בהרמה של חפצים כבדים
הכאב מחמיר בשכיבה על הגב
explanation:
**Lumbar spinal stenosis** is described in Hazzard 8e as worsening with extension and prone lying and improving with flexion and supine lying. The official historical answer is preserved alongside that source discrepancy (Hazzard 8e, p. 1632).

**A. Pain worsens on moving from lying to sitting.** Wrong, the source explicitly says lumbar stenosis should not produce pain during that transition (p. 1632).
**B. Pain worsens when walking uphill.** Wrong, the source associates worsening with extension and downhill walking and relief with flexion. The inference is that uphill walking involving flexion is not the characteristic aggravating pattern (p. 1632).
**C. Pain worsens when lifting heavy objects.** Wrong, the source says severe pain with bending and lifting objects does not characterize the stenosis described (p. 1632).
**D. Pain worsens when lying supine.** Correct, for scoring under the official key. The eighth edition instead describes relief when supine, so the official choice must not be presented as clinically supported by that edition (p. 1632).

**Official answer: ד** (IMA final official answer key after appeals, 2020, question 59).

**Hazzard 8e — examination textbook:** Worsening with extension and prone lying, and relief with flexion and supine lying, are the eighth edition's account alongside the historical official answer (p. 1632).

**Guideline/consensus comparison (secondary source):** The version actually read is the NASS 2011 update. It describes relief with forward flexion, sitting, or recumbency; this is not a new 2026 recommendation. North American Spine Society, Diagnosis and Treatment of Degenerative Lumbar Spinal Stenosis, Definition and Natural History, Work Group Consensus Statement, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 9), https://www.spine.org/Portals/0/assets/downloads/ResearchClinicalCare/Guidelines/LumbarStenosis.pdf.

Source: Hazzard 8e, p. 1632; NASS 2011, printed p. 8 (PDF p. 9). The inherited source-versus-key discrepancy is preserved.

q: בת 93, מתהלכת עם מקל, סובלת מירידה קוגניטיבית קלה. מתגוררת עם עובדת זרה. ברקע - סוכרת עם נוירופתיה, רטינופתיה ונפרופתיה עם פינוי קריאטינין 25 מ"ל/דקה. מתלוננת על כאבים קשים בכפות הרגליים עם אופי שורף וירידה בתחושה. כל הטיפולים הבאים אפשריים לבעייתה פרט ל-
o: DULOXETINE (CYMBALTA)
PREGABALIN (LYRICA)
מריחה מקומית של CAPSAICIN (ZOSTRIX )
GABAPENTIN
explanation:
All answers accepted after appeal. IMA 2020 Subspecialty official answer key, Q100.

Official acceptance is a scoring decision. The source still distinguishes **renal dose adjustment** from avoidance and from the suitability of topical treatment (Hazzard p. 1064; Beers 2023 p. 2073).

**A. Duloxetine (Cymbalta).** Correct, for scoring, as with every option after appeal. Clinically, Beers recommends avoiding duloxetine when creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min because of increased gastrointestinal adverse effects; the clearance in this question is within that range (Beers p. 2073, Table 6).
**B. Pregabalin (Lyrica).** Correct, for scoring after appeal. Pregabalin treats neuropathic pain, but the stated renal impairment requires dose reduction because of CNS adverse effects; acceptance is not an instruction to reject every use of the drug (Hazzard p. 1064; Beers p. 2073).
**C. Topical capsaicin (Zostrix).** Correct, for scoring after appeal. Topical capsaicin is a neuropathic-pain treatment; official acceptance does not establish that it is contraindicated for this patient (Hazzard p. 1064).
**D. Gabapentin.** Correct, for scoring after appeal. It treats neuropathic pain, but the stated renal impairment requires dose reduction because of CNS adverse effects; scoring does not mean that every use is impossible (Hazzard p. 1064; Beers p. 2073).

Source: Hazzard 8e, p. 1064; AGS Beers Criteria 2023, Table 6, p. 2073 (PDF p. 22). The all-answers-accepted notice is unchanged.

q: בת 67 התקבלה למחלקה עם תמונה של HERPES ZOSTER (שלבקת חוגרת). היא מתלוננת על כאבים עזים בבית חזה. לדבריה הכאבים התחילו 5 ימים לפני הופעת הפריחה. במחלקה הוחל טיפול אנטיוירלי ב- ZOVIRAX. כל הגורמים הבאים מגבירים סיכון ל- POST HERPETIC NEURALGIA פרט ל:
o: הופעת כאב לפני פריחה
כאב חזק בזמן הפריחה
גיל מעל 70
מעורבות של INTERCOSTAL NERVE
explanation:
**Postherpetic neuralgia (PHN)** is associated with features of the acute zoster episode and with age. Prodromal pain, severe acute pain, and older age are associated with increased risk, explaining why those choices are not the requested exception (Forbes et al., sections 3.2.1, 3.3.1, 4.1). For location, the review supports increased risk with ophthalmic involvement but supplies no separate estimate establishing intercostal involvement as an independent risk factor (section 3.2.2.2).
"older age was consistently associated with PHN." (Forbes et al., section 4.1).

**A. Pain before the rash.** Wrong, this is an exception question. Prodromal pain is associated with increased risk, so this patient's preceding pain belongs among the risk factors (section 3.2.1.1).
**B. Severe pain during the rash.** Wrong, severe acute zoster pain is associated with persistent pain; the described intensity therefore cannot be chosen as the exception (section 3.2.1.2).
**C. Age over 70.** Wrong, older age is a consistent risk factor. The number in the option is not a sharp biological cutoff established by the review; the age association is why this is not the exception (section 3.3.1).
**D. Intercostal nerve involvement.** Correct, under the official key, as the exception in this list. The review supports the other three factors and ophthalmic involvement, but does not separately quantify intercostal risk. This neither excludes PHN at that site nor proves that there is no additional risk (sections 3.2.2.2, 4.1).

**Official answer:** Intercostal nerve involvement (IMA, final answer key, December 2021 examination, question 69).
The textbook describes prodromal pain and nerve involvement in zoster and the functional impact of PHN. It does not rank the four proposed risk factors or provide a source-based exclusion of each of the other three options (Hazzard 8e, pp. 1725-1727).
Note: The patient in the stem is 67, so "age over 70" is not one of her characteristics. The wording mixes an individual case with a general risk-factor list; this explanation interprets the list generally and preserves official acceptance.

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1725-1727, as qualified above; Forbes et al. Pain. 2016;157:30-54, sections 3.2.1, 3.2.2.2, 3.3.1, 4.1, doi:10.1097/j.pain.0000000000000307.
explanationReviewNote: The source supports prodromal pain and postherpetic neuralgia after zoster; reaching intercostal-nerve involvement as the exception also requires the stated comparative PHN-risk rules for the other three options, which it does not state.

q: A 75-year-old man has diabetic neuropathic pain, normal renal function, and no concurrent opioid treatment. Gabapentin is started at 100 mg at bedtime as listed in Table 68-8. Which titration approach follows that table?
o: Advance to the maintenance dose immediately after the first bedtime dose
Increase the dose gradually, guided by response and tolerability
Introduce concurrent oxycodone as the gabapentin dose is increased
Replace low-dose initiation with immediate maintenance-dose treatment
explanation:
**Low-dose initiation and gradual titration** are the table’s principles for gabapentinoids (p. 1063). It states "Initiate at lowest dose and gradually titrate" and cautions against concurrent opioid use; central nervous system adverse effects also require attention (pp. 1063–1064).

**A. Advance to the maintenance dose immediately after the first bedtime dose.** Wrong, an immediate increase to maintenance dosing conflicts with the table’s gradual titration instruction (p. 1063).
**B. Increase the dose gradually, guided by response and tolerability.** Correct, gradual adjustment follows the stated approach, with response and adverse effects informing the clinical application (pp. 1063–1064).
**C. Introduce concurrent oxycodone as the gabapentin dose is increased.** Wrong, the table advises avoiding gabapentinoids in patients with concurrent opioid use, so introducing oxycodone conflicts with that instruction (p. 1063).
**D. Replace low-dose initiation with immediate maintenance-dose treatment.** Wrong, immediate maintenance-dose treatment abandons both low-dose initiation and gradual titration (p. 1063).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1063, 1064.

q: Why does Hazzard recommend starting opioid treatment at a lower dose in older adults?
o: Faster medication clearance increases accumulation and adverse effects
Reduced medication clearance increases accumulation and adverse effects
Reduced medication clearance shortens exposure and reduces adverse effects
Faster medication clearance prolongs exposure and reduces adverse effects
explanation:
**Reduced drug clearance** can increase susceptibility to opioid accumulation in older adults, even without diagnosed renal disease. The chapter also describes a longer time to elimination and risks including sedation and respiratory depression, providing the rationale for a lower starting dose (p. 1060).
"given reduced renal function and medication clearance even without renal disease, older adults may be more susceptible to the accumulation of opioids" (p. 1060).

**A. Faster medication clearance increases accumulation and adverse effects.** Wrong, the source identifies reduced, not faster, clearance as a contributor to accumulation (p. 1060).
**B. Reduced medication clearance increases accumulation and adverse effects.** Correct, this links the documented clearance change to accumulation and the adverse-effect concern underlying lower initial doses (p. 1060).
**C. Reduced medication clearance shortens exposure and reduces adverse effects.** Wrong, reduced clearance is associated with susceptibility to accumulation and a longer elimination time, not shortened exposure (p. 1060).
**D. Faster medication clearance prolongs exposure and reduces adverse effects.** Wrong, the source describes slower clearance with longer elimination and increased adverse-effect risk; faster clearance with fewer effects is not its rationale for lower dosing (p. 1060).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1060.

q: גבר בן 75 עם דמנציה מתקדמת וכאב סיבי מנוון, אינו מוטל מדיבור, דורס טבליות. רופא הבית מעוניין להתחיל משכך כאב. מה הדרך הטובה ביותר?
o: אופיואיד בתחזוקה PO או דחוף ללשון
טלאי פנטניל טרנסדרמי ודוקומנטציית החלטות מוקדמות
הזרקות בדלתא עמוד שדרה לשליטה בכאב
המתנה עד שיוכל לבטא כאב בדיבור
explanation:
## הסבר קליני

**התשובה הנכונה היא ב' - טלאי פנטניל טרנסדרמי ודוקומנטציית החלטות מוקדמות**

המטופל סובל מ**כאב כרוני סיבי מנוון** הדורש טיפול משכך יעיל, אך **הדיספגיה** (קושי בבליעת טבליות) מגבילה את האפשרויות הטיפוליות.

**טלאי פנטניל טרנסדרמי** הוא הבחירה האופטימלית כי:
- מתאים ל**כאב כרוני מתמשך** (לא לכאב חריף)
- **אינו דורש בליעה** - יישום חיצוני על העור
- מספק **שחרור ממושך** (החלפה כל 72 שעות)
- **נוח למטופלי דמנציה** שאינם משתפי פעולה עם תרופות פומיות
- **דוקומנטציה של החלטות מוקדמות** חיונית בדמנציה מתקדמת

**פסילת תשובות שגויות:**
- **א'**: אופיואידים פומיים או תת-לשוניים - בעייתיים בגלל הדיספגיה וקושי בשיתוף פעולה
- **ג'**: הזרקות אפידורליות - פולשניות מדי, לא מעשיות לטיפול ממושך בבית
- **ד'**: המתנה - **לא אתית**, גורמת לסבל מיותר; כאב ניתן להערכה גם ב**מטופלים לא מדברים** (סולמות התנהגותיים)

**(Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine, 8th Edition)**
retiredReason: Hazzard 8e (marked), p.1061 Table 68-6: transdermal fentanyl should be avoided in opioid-naive patients. Initial analgesic choice is unsupported without opioid tolerance, and garbled alternatives prevent a single source-supported answer.

q: A 75-year-old man with severe cancer pain and reduced kidney function is starting an opioid. Which dosing principle addresses his vulnerability to drug accumulation?
o: Use a usual starting dose and titrate according to pain intensity
Use a lower starting dose and titrate with close safety monitoring
Use an increased starting dose and titrate according to pain intensity
Use a usual starting dose and extend the interval between reviews
explanation:
**Reduced clearance** increases susceptibility to opioid accumulation in older adults (p. 1060). Hazzard recommends "prescribing the lowest effective dose possible" and close early follow-up; it also advises lower starting doses because of increased adverse-effect risk (p. 1060).

**A. Use a usual starting dose and titrate according to pain intensity.** Wrong, pain response matters, but this plan omits the lower-dose and monitoring precautions needed for accumulation risk (p. 1060).
**B. Use a lower starting dose and titrate with close safety monitoring.** Correct, lower starting exposure and close follow-up match the source’s prescribing precautions for older adults with reduced clearance (p. 1060).
**C. Use an increased starting dose and titrate according to pain intensity.** Wrong, an increased starting dose conflicts with the source’s recommendation to start lower because of adverse-effect risk (p. 1060).
**D. Use a usual starting dose and extend the interval between reviews.** Wrong, less frequent early review conflicts with the recommendation for close follow-up after opioid initiation (p. 1060).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1060.

q: An opioid is being considered for an older adult with persistent pain that has not improved with conservative treatment. Which principle should guide selection and initiation?
o: Match opioid potency to pain severity and start cautiously
Use a young-adult starting dose to compensate for aging physiology
Escalate treatment rapidly before discussing expected risks and benefits
Escalate a combination product without considering its nonopioid component
explanation:
**Opioid initiation** must account for pain severity and the increased susceptibility of older adults to adverse effects. Hazzard recommends that clinicians “start opioids at a lower dose” because side-effect risk is greater in older adults (p. 1060). It also requires discussion of risks and benefits and notes that the nonopioid component limits the maximum dose of combination products (p. 1060).

**A. Match opioid potency to pain severity and start cautiously.** Correct, potency is selected in relation to pain severity, with a lower starting dose because older adults are more susceptible to adverse effects (p. 1060).
**B. Use a young-adult starting dose to compensate for aging physiology.** Wrong, the source advises lower initial dosing in older adults, not using a younger patient’s dose to compensate for aging (p. 1060).
**C. Escalate treatment rapidly before discussing expected risks and benefits.** Wrong, the source calls for a thorough risks-and-benefits discussion before considering opioid treatment after conservative treatment failure (p. 1060).
**D. Escalate a combination product without considering its nonopioid component.** Wrong, the maximum combination-product dose is typically determined by its acetaminophen, NSAID, or aspirin component (p. 1060).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1060.

q: An older woman taking sertraline needs analgesia after a fracture, and tramadol is being considered. Which pharmacologic consideration explains particular caution with this combination?
o: Tramadol's serotonergic action favors combining it with an antidepressant for protection
Tramadol's serotonergic action counteracts the effect of the patient's sertraline
Tramadol's serotonergic action is a reason to avoid the combination
Tramadol's serotonergic action favors increasing the doses of both medicines
explanation:
**Tramadol** has opioid-receptor agonist and serotonin-reuptake-inhibiting actions. Hazzard advises avoiding it with other serotonergic drugs; sertraline is listed among selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, connecting that precaution to this patient (pp. 929, 1061).
"Acts both as an opioid receptor agonist" (p. 1061).
"Avoid in patients with other serotonergic drugs or history of seizures" (p. 1061).

**A. Tramadol's serotonergic action favors combining it with an antidepressant for protection.** Wrong, the source advises avoidance with serotonergic drugs rather than using the combination for a protective effect (p. 1061).
**B. Tramadol's serotonergic action counteracts the effect of the patient's sertraline.** Wrong, the source treats serotonergic coadministration as a reason for avoidance, not as a way to counteract the other drug (p. 1061).
**C. Tramadol's serotonergic action is a reason to avoid the combination.** Correct, sertraline belongs to the listed SSRI group, and the tramadol entry advises avoiding other serotonergic drugs (pp. 929, 1061).
**D. Tramadol's serotonergic action favors increasing the doses of both medicines.** Wrong, increasing both doses does not follow the source's explicit advice to avoid this combination (p. 1061).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1061, 929.

q: An 81-year-old woman with diabetes, stage 4 CKD, and peripheral neuropathy has severe burning foot pain despite gabapentin and acetaminophen. She has also developed confusion and fallen. Which step best applies Hazzard's medication-safety principles before adding or escalating treatment?
o: Increase gabapentin before reviewing its relationship to the new confusion
Add another centrally acting analgesic before reviewing the existing regimen
Review gabapentin for CNS adverse effects before further dose escalation
Continue the current regimen while treating the confusion as unrelated to medication
explanation:
**Gabapentinoids** can cause central nervous system depression, fatigue, dizziness, and disorientation. Hazzard advises considering medication effects when new symptoms arise and deprescribing through dose reduction or cessation where appropriate; the source does not establish an exact replacement dose for this patient (pp. 314–315, 1064). "These medications have a high risk for side effects such as central nervous system depression, fatigue, dizziness, and disorientation." (p. 1064).

**A. Increase gabapentin before reviewing its relationship to the new confusion.** Wrong, escalation before review overlooks adverse effects that are relevant to the new confusion and fall (pp. 314, 1064).
**B. Add another centrally acting analgesic before reviewing the existing regimen.** Wrong, adding treatment before reviewing the existing regimen leaves a potential medication-related contributor unassessed (pp. 314, 1064).
**C. Review gabapentin for CNS adverse effects before further dose escalation.** Correct, this considers a documented adverse-effect pattern and uses the source's individualized deprescribing approach (pp. 314–315, 1064).
**D. Continue the current regimen while treating the confusion as unrelated to medication.** Wrong, the documented potential for disorientation makes an assumption of no medication contribution unjustified without review (pp. 314, 1064).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1064, 314, 315.

q: Medications are being considered for a woman with neuropathic pain and a creatinine clearance of 24 mL/min. Which recommendation matches the renal-adjustment table in the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria?
o: Use pregabalin at the usual dose without renal dose reduction
Avoid duloxetine because of the degree of kidney impairment
Use gabapentin at the usual dose without renal dose reduction
Use extended-release tramadol at the usual prescribed dose
explanation:
**Duloxetine avoidance** is recommended below a creatinine clearance of 30 mL/min because of increased gastrointestinal adverse effects. The same table recommends dose reduction for gabapentin and pregabalin below 60 mL/min, and avoidance of extended-release tramadol below 30 mL/min. (p. 2073)
"Duloxetine <30 Increased GI adverse effects (nausea, diarrhea) Avoid" (p. 2073)
"Gabapentin <60 CNS adverse effects Reduce dose" (p. 2073)

**A. Use pregabalin at the usual dose without renal dose reduction.** Wrong, the table recommends reducing pregabalin at a clearance below 60 mL/min, which includes the value in this stem. (p. 2073)
**B. Avoid duloxetine because of the degree of kidney impairment.** Correct, the stated clearance is below the threshold at which the table recommends avoiding duloxetine. (p. 2073)
**C. Use gabapentin at the usual dose without renal dose reduction.** Wrong, the table recommends reducing gabapentin at a clearance below 60 mL/min, which includes the value in this stem. (p. 2073)
**D. Use extended-release tramadol at the usual prescribed dose.** Wrong, extended-release tramadol is listed for avoidance below 30 mL/min; the immediate-release formulation has a separate dose-reduction recommendation. (p. 2073)

Source: 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, Table 6, p. 2073.

q: A 79-year-old woman has pain after hip-fracture surgery despite oxycodone. She has mild cognitive impairment and reduced renal function, without known liver disease. The team is reassessing her pain and wants to reduce opioid exposure. Which addition fits the multimodal approach described in Hazzard?
o: Add clonazepam and consider an appropriate regional technique
Add methocarbamol and consider an appropriate regional technique
Add amitriptyline and consider an appropriate regional technique
Add acetaminophen and consider an appropriate regional technique
explanation:
**Multimodal analgesia** aims to reduce opioid use through complementary approaches, including acetaminophen and selected regional anesthesia techniques. The source cautions against benzodiazepines with opioids, identifies limited tolerated efficacy of methocarbamol in older adults, and warns about the anticholinergic burden of tricyclic antidepressants (pp. 1062-1064).
"ERAS protocols attempt to minimize the use of opioids and offer opioid-sparing techniques such as intravenous or oral acetaminophen" (p. 1062).
"neuraxial and peripheral regional anesthesia regional techniques for select surgeries" (p. 1062).

**A. Add clonazepam and consider an appropriate regional technique.** Wrong, the table advises avoiding benzodiazepines with concurrent opioids because of sedation and falls (p. 1064).
**B. Add methocarbamol and consider an appropriate regional technique.** Wrong, the table advises avoiding methocarbamol because efficacy is limited at doses tolerated by older adults (p. 1064).
**C. Add amitriptyline and consider an appropriate regional technique.** Wrong, amitriptyline has potent anticholinergic activity with possible cognitive adverse effects, making it a poor fit for this proposed addition (pp. 1063-1064).
**D. Add acetaminophen and consider an appropriate regional technique.** Correct, acetaminophen and selected regional anesthesia techniques are explicitly included among opioid-sparing approaches (p. 1062).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 1062, 1064.

q: An 82-year-old woman starts gabapentin for neuropathic pain and develops somnolence, dizziness, and unsteadiness. Evaluation shows no orthostatic fall in blood pressure. Which recognized pair of effects fits these new symptoms?
o: Increased alertness and improved orientation
Central nervous system depression and improved orientation
Central nervous system depression and disorientation
Increased alertness and disorientation
explanation:
**Gabapentinoids** are used for neuropathic pain but have central nervous system adverse effects (p. 1064). The source lists "central nervous system depression, fatigue, dizziness, and disorientation"; the new symptoms fit that adverse-effect profile without proving drug causation (p. 1064).

**A. Increased alertness and improved orientation.** Wrong, increased alertness and improved orientation are inconsistent with the listed depression and disorientation (p. 1064).
**B. Central nervous system depression and improved orientation.** Wrong, central nervous system depression fits, but improved orientation does not match the listed disorientation (p. 1064).
**C. Central nervous system depression and disorientation.** Correct, both effects are included in the adverse-effect profile of gabapentin and related anticonvulsants (p. 1064).
**D. Increased alertness and disorientation.** Wrong, disorientation fits, but increased alertness conflicts with the listed central nervous system depression (p. 1064).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1064.

q: Duloxetine is being considered for a 76-year-old man with neuropathic pain and a calculated creatinine clearance of 24 mL/min. Which approach follows the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria?
o: Start the usual dose and monitor kidney function during treatment
Start a low dose and increase it gradually during treatment
Avoid duloxetine in the range of kidney function described
Give duloxetine intermittently while retaining the usual dose per administration
explanation:
For **duloxetine**, Beers recommends avoidance when creatinine clearance is below 30 mL/min. The table gives the rationale "Increased GI adverse effects (nausea, diarrhea)" and the recommendation "Avoid" (Table 6, p. 2073).

**A. Start the usual dose and monitor kidney function during treatment.** Wrong, at this creatinine clearance, the recommendation is avoidance; renal monitoring does not substitute for that recommendation (p. 2073).
**B. Start a low dose and increase it gradually during treatment.** Wrong, the table specifies avoidance rather than initiation at a reduced dose with subsequent escalation (p. 2073).
**C. Avoid duloxetine in the range of kidney function described.** Correct, the patient’s creatinine clearance is below the stated threshold, where increased gastrointestinal adverse effects support avoidance (p. 2073).
**D. Give duloxetine intermittently while retaining the usual dose per administration.** Wrong, intermittent administration is not the listed renal adjustment; the recommendation at this clearance is avoidance (p. 2073).

Source: AGS Beers 2023, pp. 2073.

q: A 78-year-old woman with cognitive impairment and recurrent falls needs an opioid for postoperative pain. Which risk warrants active monitoring after treatment begins?
o: Central nervous system depression and sedation during treatment
Acceleration of intestinal motility during treatment
Shortening of drug elimination time with aging
Improvement of cognitive stability as the drug accumulates
explanation:
**Opioid adverse effects** in older adults include central nervous system depression, sedation, respiratory depression, and constipation. Age-related changes in distribution and clearance can prolong elimination, and cognitive impairment increases concern about opioid-induced confusion (p. 1060).
"older patients are at risk for side effects such as central nervous system depression, sedation, respiratory depression, and constipation." (p. 1060).

**A. Central nervous system depression and sedation during treatment.** Correct, these are explicitly listed opioid adverse effects in older patients (p. 1060).
**B. Acceleration of intestinal motility during treatment.** Wrong, the described bowel concern is constipation, not accelerated motility (p. 1060).
**C. Shortening of drug elimination time with aging.** Wrong, the source describes a longer elimination time rather than faster clearance (p. 1060).
**D. Improvement of cognitive stability as the drug accumulates.** Wrong, accumulation and opioid-induced confusion are concerns, not evidence of cognitive stabilization (p. 1060).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1060.

q: An older woman takes duloxetine regularly and is prescribed tramadol for postoperative pain. Before increasing analgesia, which approach follows Hazzard's advice on the serotonergic drug combination?
o: Avoid combining tramadol with the existing serotonergic medication.
Increase tramadol while continuing the existing serotonergic medication.
Change tramadol to extended release while continuing the existing medication.
Divide the tramadol dose while continuing the existing serotonergic medication.
explanation:
**Tramadol** acts both as an opioid receptor agonist and a serotonin-reuptake inhibitor (p. 1061). The table advises: "Avoid in patients with other serotonergic drugs or history of seizures" (p. 1061). Duloxetine is listed among serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (p. 930), so the combination falls within that warning.

**A. Avoid combining tramadol with the existing serotonergic medication.** Correct, this applies the instruction to avoid tramadol with another serotonergic drug (pp. 930, 1061).
**B. Increase tramadol while continuing the existing serotonergic medication.** Wrong, escalating tramadol retains the combination the source advises avoiding (p. 1061).
**C. Change tramadol to extended release while continuing the existing medication.** Wrong, changing the formulation does not remove the combination of tramadol with a serotonergic drug (p. 1061).
**D. Divide the tramadol dose while continuing the existing serotonergic medication.** Wrong, dividing doses leaves the warned-against combination in place (p. 1061).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 930, 1061.

q: A patient with advanced dementia and a painful vulvar mass cannot reliably answer pain questions. She grimaces during personal care. How should her pain be assessed?
o: Determine pain intensity from the severity of the lesion on examination
Combine a nonverbal observational pain scale with caregiver information
Favor a verbal pain score over observation despite inconsistent answers
Defer pain assessment until communication supports reliable verbal scoring
explanation:
**Pain assessment** should adapt to limitations in communication. Hazzard states that "a nonverbal observational pain scale may be indicated to better assess their pain" when patients have difficulty responding (p. 1058). Family and caregivers should also provide information in cognitive impairment or dementia; examination remains part of assessment rather than a substitute for these sources.

**A. Determine pain intensity from the severity of the lesion on examination.** Wrong, examination is part of the assessment, but lesion severity does not replace the recommended observational and caregiver information when self-report is unreliable (p. 1058).
**B. Combine a nonverbal observational pain scale with caregiver information.** Correct, this combines the two approaches specifically recommended for difficulty answering pain questions and cognitive impairment (p. 1058).
**C. Favor a verbal pain score over observation despite inconsistent answers.** Wrong, the communication problem calls for observational assessment rather than privileging an unreliable verbal score (p. 1058).
**D. Defer pain assessment until communication supports reliable verbal scoring.** Wrong, the source supplies an observational route when the patient cannot respond; postponing assessment until verbal scoring becomes reliable fails to use it (p. 1058).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1058.

q: A 79-year-old woman with diabetes and neuropathic foot pain has not benefited from ibuprofen. Her creatinine clearance is 22 mL/min, and serum creatinine rose after treatment began. According to the 2023 AGS Beers Criteria, which medication change is appropriate before choosing alternative analgesia?
o: Reduce ibuprofen and continue daily oral treatment
Stop ibuprofen and choose treatment outside systemic NSAIDs
Replace ibuprofen with oral celecoxib and monitor kidney function
Replace ibuprofen with injected ketorolac and monitor kidney function
explanation:
**Systemic NSAIDs in renal impairment** are addressed as a group, including nonselective and COX-2 selective drugs and oral and parenteral formulations (p. 2073). Below a creatinine clearance of 30 mL/min, the recommendation is to avoid them because they "May increase the risk of acute kidney injury and a further decline in kidney function" (p. 2073).

**A. Reduce ibuprofen and continue daily oral treatment.** Wrong, the criterion recommends avoidance rather than dose reduction at this level of kidney function (p. 2073).
**B. Stop ibuprofen and choose treatment outside systemic NSAIDs.** Correct, this follows the recommendation to avoid systemic NSAIDs at the stated creatinine clearance, without presuming a particular replacement is suitable (p. 2073).
**C. Replace ibuprofen with oral celecoxib and monitor kidney function.** Wrong, Celecoxib is included among the COX-2 selective NSAIDs covered by the criterion, so this substitution does not avoid the renal-risk category (p. 2073).
**D. Replace ibuprofen with injected ketorolac and monitor kidney function.** Wrong, Ketorolac and parenteral NSAIDs are included; changing the route does not remove the avoidance recommendation (p. 2073).

Source: AGS Beers 2023, pp. 2073.

q: A woman has taken lorazepam daily for months alongside an opioid and has sedation and falls. A decision has been made to reduce the benzodiazepine. Which discontinuation approach matches Hazzard?
o: Gradually taper the dose because of the risk of physical dependence
Abruptly stop the dose because of the risk of physical dependence
Temporarily increase the dose because of the risk of physical dependence
Continue the current dose because of the risk of physical dependence
explanation:
**Physical dependence** can develop with daily benzodiazepine use. The source recommends gradual tapering to avoid withdrawal symptoms, which is relevant when discontinuation is planned after months of treatment (p. 1065).
"Older adults taking daily benzodiazepines for more than 30 days may develop physiologic dependence and should be gradually tapered to avoid risk of withdrawal symptoms." (p. 1065).

**A. Gradually taper the dose because of the risk of physical dependence.** Correct, tapering is the recommended approach to reducing withdrawal risk after sustained daily use (p. 1065).
**B. Abruptly stop the dose because of the risk of physical dependence.** Wrong, abrupt cessation omits the gradual reduction recommended to avoid withdrawal symptoms (p. 1065).
**C. Temporarily increase the dose because of the risk of physical dependence.** Wrong, increasing the dose does not implement the recommended taper when stopping treatment (p. 1065).
**D. Continue the current dose because of the risk of physical dependence.** Wrong, dependence calls for a tapering strategy when discontinuation is chosen, not indefinite continuation of the current dose (p. 1065).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1065.

q: A 77-year-old woman with hypertension, diabetes, osteoarthritis, and newly diagnosed mild cognitive impairment takes metformin 1000 mg twice daily, lisinopril 20 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, celecoxib 200 mg daily, and acetaminophen 500 mg four times daily. She develops ankle edema, an eight-pound weight gain over two weeks, and worsening knee pain. Blood pressure is 165/95 mm Hg, pulse 88/min, and creatinine has risen from 1.1 to 1.4 mg/dL. Which change directly removes an NSAID exposure while retaining a non-NSAID analgesic strategy?
o: Stop celecoxib and reassess the acetaminophen regimen
Stop amlodipine and add hydrochlorothiazide
Stop lisinopril and start losartan
Continue the analgesics and add furosemide 20 mg daily
explanation:
**NSAIDs can contribute to sodium retention and edema**, and their use also warrants attention to cardiovascular and kidney risks. Acetaminophen is a non-NSAID analgesic option, with attention to total dose and hepatic risk; the vignette does not prove that one drug explains every new finding (pp. 589, 1062).
"Even in the absence of heart failure, these drugs may cause sodium retention and subsequent edema." (p. 589).

**A. Stop celecoxib and reassess the acetaminophen regimen.** Correct, this removes celecoxib, the COX-2-selective NSAID, while reassessing a non-NSAID pain treatment (p. 1062).
**B. Stop amlodipine and add hydrochlorothiazide.** Wrong, this leaves the NSAID exposure in place, so it does not perform the action asked for (pp. 589, 1062).
**C. Stop lisinopril and start losartan.** Wrong, changing renin-angiotensin therapy leaves celecoxib exposure unaddressed (p. 1062).
**D. Continue the analgesics and add furosemide 20 mg daily.** Wrong, adding a diuretic does not remove the possible medication contributor identified in the question (pp. 589, 1062).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 589, 1062.

q: A 78-year-old man requires analgesia after hip-fracture surgery. The team wants to reduce opioid exposure while maintaining pain treatment. Which principle is consistent with enhanced recovery after surgery?
o: Rely on increasing the opioid dose as the central analgesic strategy
Postpone analgesic treatment to reduce exposure to medicines after surgery
Combine analgesic approaches while minimizing opioid use after surgery
Use one analgesic mechanism to reduce the range of postoperative medicines
explanation:
**Enhanced recovery after surgery** uses multimodal analgesia to minimize opioid use while treating postoperative pain. Opioids still have an important role, but their adverse effects, particularly in older adults, motivate opioid-sparing approaches (p. 1062).
"The mainstay of ERAS protocols is the judicious use of multimodal analgesia." (p. 1062).

**A. Rely on increasing the opioid dose as the central analgesic strategy.** Wrong, relying on opioid escalation does not implement the opioid-sparing multimodal approach described in the source (p. 1062).
**B. Postpone analgesic treatment to reduce exposure to medicines after surgery.** Wrong, the approach provides analgesia through several methods; it does not seek lower exposure by leaving postoperative pain untreated (p. 1062).
**C. Combine analgesic approaches while minimizing opioid use after surgery.** Correct, this combines the central multimodal principle with the goal of minimizing opioid use (p. 1062).
**D. Use one analgesic mechanism to reduce the range of postoperative medicines.** Wrong, restricting treatment to one mechanism misses the multimodal approach that forms the mainstay of the protocol (p. 1062).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1062.

q: A patient continues to have chronic pain after the initial injury has subsided. Which explanation does Hazzard describe?
o: Reduced strength of pain pathways together with increased sensory inhibition
Altered neural connections and sensitivity to stimuli after the injury
Restoration of pain pathways to their previous state as tissue heals
Reduced brain processing of pain through increased inhibitory pathways
explanation:
**Maladaptive neuroplasticity** can sustain pain signaling after the initial injury has subsided. Hazzard describes altered connections and sensitivity, with stronger pain pathways and reduced inhibitory pathways contributing to increased pain processing (p. 1056).
"the nervous system will continue to send signals for pain even after the initial injury has subsided." (p. 1056).
"neural connections are rewired and sensitivity to stimuli changes in response to an initial injury." (p. 1056).

**A. Reduced strength of pain pathways together with increased sensory inhibition.** Wrong, the source describes increased synaptic strength of pain pathways and reduced inhibition, not weaker pain pathways with greater inhibition (p. 1056).
**B. Altered neural connections and sensitivity to stimuli after the injury.** Correct, this matches the changes in neural connections and stimulus sensitivity used to explain persistent pain signaling (p. 1056).
**C. Restoration of pain pathways to their previous state as tissue heals.** Wrong, the source describes continued pain signals after the initial injury subsides, so tissue recovery does not establish restoration of the prior neural state (p. 1056).
**D. Reduced brain processing of pain through increased inhibitory pathways.** Wrong, the described maladaptive change increases pain processing and reduces inhibitory pathways; the proposed combination does not explain that process (p. 1056).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1056.

q: A care-home resident with dementia and knee osteoarthritis cannot answer pain questions consistently and grimaces with movement. Staff report reduced activity. How should pain be assessed before treatment is adjusted?
o: Favor a general question about wellbeing and base the assessment on the conversation
Favor detailed complex questions and base the assessment on her verbal formulation
Favor the first visit’s pain score and base subsequent assessment on that earlier score
Favor simple questions and combine observation with family and caregiver information
explanation:
**Pain assessment in dementia** should still attempt self-report while adapting to difficulties answering questions. The source recommends simple, direct questions, an observational pain scale when needed, and information from family or caregivers; repeated assessment evaluates treatment benefit (p. 1058).
"In older adults, the line of questioning should be simple and transparent." (p. 1058).
"For patients with difficulty responding to pain questions, a nonverbal observational pain scale may be indicated to better assess their pain." (p. 1058).

**A. Favor a general question about wellbeing and base the assessment on the conversation.** Wrong, a specific question about pain may be more informative than a general question about wellbeing (p. 1058).
**B. Favor detailed complex questions and base the assessment on her verbal formulation.** Wrong, the recommended questions are simple and transparent, rather than linguistically complex (p. 1058).
**C. Favor the first visit’s pain score and base subsequent assessment on that earlier score.** Wrong, pain characteristics should be assessed regularly at follow-up rather than carrying forward an initial rating (p. 1058).
**D. Favor simple questions and combine observation with family and caregiver information.** Correct, this combines the recommended adaptations when self-report is difficult (p. 1058).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1058.

q: An 84-year-old nursing-home resident with advanced dementia and hip osteoarthritis cries during routine care, moans during transfers, and resists bathing. Her PAINAD score is 7/10 despite scheduled acetaminophen 650 mg three times daily. Her daughter, the health care proxy, fears opioid addiction. Which educational message about persistent pain in dementia is supported by Hazzard?
o: Explain that dementia makes persistent pain unsuitable for an opioid trial
Discuss a monitored opioid trial for pain despite current treatment
Explain that age protects against opioid misuse during an analgesic trial
Explain that cognitive impairment reduces medication errors during opioid use
explanation:
**Persistent pain in dementia** warrants assessment and a stepwise treatment discussion (pp. 1048, 1058). "Opioids may be tried for nonresponders." This must include risks and monitoring, because cognitive impairment can increase medication errors and opioid-induced confusion (pp. 1048, 1060).

**A. Explain that dementia makes persistent pain unsuitable for an opioid trial.** Wrong, the source explicitly permits an opioid trial for nonresponders in its dementia pain discussion (p. 1048).
**B. Discuss a monitored opioid trial for pain despite current treatment.** Correct, discussing a monitored trial follows the stepwise approach while addressing the risks described for older adults (pp. 1048, 1060).
**C. Explain that age protects against opioid misuse during an analgesic trial.** Wrong, the source states older adults are not immune to harmful consequences of opioid misuse, so age is not protection (p. 1060).
**D. Explain that cognitive impairment reduces medication errors during opioid use.** Wrong, cognitive impairment increases, rather than reduces, the risk of medication-related errors and opioid-induced confusion (p. 1060).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1048, 1060.

q: A 77-year-old man in rehabilitation after hip-fracture repair has constant pain at rest and with movement. As-needed immediate-release oxycodone relieves it, but late administration allows pain to recur between doses. Which dosing strategy fits this pain pattern in Hazzard?
o: Administer the medication after the pain has peaked each time
Concentrate medication administration at night despite daytime pain
Reserve medication administration for the daytime physiotherapy sessions
Plan scheduled administration and titrate treatment to comfort
explanation:
Hazzard distinguishes **constant pain** from episodic pain when describing immediate-release opioid use. For immediate-release oxycodone, the table states: "Titrate to comfort: continuous use for constant pain and intermittent use for episodic pain" (Table 68-6, p. 1061). The constant pain described here fits the continuous-use approach (p. 1061).

**A. Administer the medication after the pain has peaked each time.** Wrong, waiting for each pain peak is episodic administration, whereas the source associates constant pain with continuous use (p. 1061).
**B. Concentrate medication administration at night despite daytime pain.** Wrong, nighttime-focused administration does not address the constant daytime pain specified in the stem (p. 1061).
**C. Reserve medication administration for the daytime physiotherapy sessions.** Wrong, limiting administration to physiotherapy does not cover the constant pain at rest described in the stem (p. 1061).
**D. Plan scheduled administration and titrate treatment to comfort.** Correct, scheduled use with titration to comfort applies the table’s approach to constant pain (p. 1061).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1061.

q: גבר בן 85 נמצא ביום 3 של שיקום אקוטי לאחר החלפת שני ברכיים. יש לו CKD stage 3 (eGFR 45), CHF (EF 40%), ואוסטאופורוזיס. הוא מוטיבציה אך מפתח כאב קשה (9/10) עם כיפוף הברך מעבר ל-70 מעלות, המגביל את התקדמות הטיפול. טיפול אנלגטי נוכחי: acetaminophen 1g TID, celecoxib 200mg יומי, oxycodone 5mg q6h PRN (משתמש ב-3-4 מנות ביום). אשתו שואלת על תרופות כאב חזקות יותר. מהי ההתאמה המתאימה ביותר?
o: להעלות oxycodone ל-7.5mg q6h PRN
להוסיף gabapentin 100mg TID
להחליף celecoxib ב-naproxen 250mg BID
להוסיף tramadol 25mg q6h
explanation: Retired: Table 68-8 (p1063) says to avoid gabapentinoids with concurrent opioid use and lists renal impairment as a contraindication. The previous explanation claiming no added opioid risk was wrong. The fixed stem and these dosing alternatives do not establish a unique book-supported choice; this question is no longer served in Practice.
retiredReason: Book p1063 contradicts adding gabapentin with concurrent opioids and renal impairment; this stem does not establish a single best alternative dosing change.

q: A 77-year-old woman with dementia is undergoing rehabilitation after hip-fracture repair. She becomes agitated when staff move the affected limb and cannot answer pain questions consistently. Which approach is appropriate for assessing pain?
o: Use an observational pain scale and obtain additional information from caregivers
Defer pain assessment until language improves enough for a detailed interview
Use broad questions about general well-being instead of specific pain questions
Require completion of a numerical intensity scale before interpreting pain symptoms
explanation:
**Pain assessment** must account for difficulty communicating in dementia (p. 1058). Simple, specific questions are recommended, and an observational scale provides an alternative when responses are difficult: "For patients with difficulty responding to pain questions, a nonverbal observational pain scale may be indicated to better assess their pain." (p. 1058). Caregiver information supplements the assessment rather than requiring consistent verbal answers (p. 1058).

**A. Use an observational pain scale and obtain additional information from caregivers.** Correct, the source recommends an observational scale for difficulty answering questions and information from family or caregivers in cognitive impairment (p. 1058).
**B. Defer pain assessment until language improves enough for a detailed interview.** Wrong, the source provides an observational approach for this communication difficulty; postponing assessment until a detailed interview is possible leaves that route unused (p. 1058).
**C. Use broad questions about general well-being instead of specific pain questions.** Wrong, the source recommends simple, transparent pain questions and specifically contrasts asking whether something hurts with a general question about well-being (p. 1058).
**D. Require completion of a numerical intensity scale before interpreting pain symptoms.** Wrong, a required numerical response does not accommodate the stated communication problem; the source allows nonverbal observation and caregiver information (p. 1058).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1058.

q: An opioid-naive 85-year-old woman with dementia and chronic kidney disease has persistent pain limiting rehabilitation despite nonopioid treatment. After assessment, a trial of an opioid is chosen. Which initiation principle matches Hazzard?
o: Begin with an extended-release formulation to reduce dosing frequency
Begin at the usual younger-adult dose for rapid analgesia
Begin at a low dose with close monitoring of response
Begin treatment and defer adverse-effect assessment to a distant visit
explanation:
**Low-dose opioid initiation** with close follow-up is emphasized for older adults. Reduced renal function and clearance can promote accumulation, while cognitive impairment adds risk of medication errors and opioid-induced confusion (p. 1060).
"prescribing immediate-release opioids" (p. 1060).

**A. Begin with an extended-release formulation to reduce dosing frequency.** Wrong, the source emphasizes immediate-release opioids for initiation rather than an extended-release starting strategy (p. 1060).
**B. Begin at the usual younger-adult dose for rapid analgesia.** Wrong, it recommends lower starting doses in older adults because of their increased risk of adverse effects (p. 1060).
**C. Begin at a low dose with close monitoring of response.** Correct, low-dose initiation and close follow-up follow the stated principles in the setting of renal and cognitive vulnerability (p. 1060; application).
**D. Begin treatment and defer adverse-effect assessment to a distant visit.** Wrong, deferring assessment conflicts with the recommendation for close follow-up after starting therapy (p. 1060).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1060.

q: An older patient with severe persistent pain is being considered for opioid analgesia. Which principle is appropriate when starting treatment in an older adult?
o: Start at a lower dose because of increased adverse-effect risk
Start at a higher dose because elimination takes longer
Start at a higher dose because of susceptibility to respiratory depression
Start at the usual younger-adult dose because clearance is faster
explanation:
**Age-related changes in opioid handling** can prolong elimination and increase adverse-effect risk. Hazzard therefore recommends starting at a lower dose in older adults rather than treating delayed clearance as a reason for a higher dose (p. 1060).
"Because of the increased risk of side effects in older adults, it is recommended to start opioids at a lower dose" (p. 1060).
"changes in drug distribution and a longer time for elimination." (p. 1060).

**A. Start at a lower dose because of increased adverse-effect risk.** Correct, the source links the recommendation for a lower starting dose to the increased risk of adverse effects in older adults (p. 1060).
**B. Start at a higher dose because elimination takes longer.** Wrong, longer elimination time is part of the reason for greater adverse-effect risk, so it does not justify the proposed dose increase (p. 1060).
**C. Start at a higher dose because of susceptibility to respiratory depression.** Wrong, respiratory depression is a harm to account for when dosing; greater susceptibility supports caution rather than a higher starting dose (p. 1060).
**D. Start at the usual younger-adult dose because clearance is faster.** Wrong, the source describes reduced clearance and a longer time for elimination, not the faster clearance assumed in this option (p. 1060).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1060.

q: An 80-year-old woman with postoperative back pain and chronic neuropathic pain is receiving an opioid. The team considers adding gabapentin. Which risk explains caution with the combination?
o: Increased neuronal conduction with arousal and disturbed sleep
Reduced opioid effect with development of pharmacologic tolerance
Accelerated opioid clearance with loss of analgesic effect
Combined depressant effects on the central nervous system
explanation:
**Gabapentinoids** can cause central nervous system depression, dizziness, and disorientation. Hazzard specifically advises caution when combining them with opioids because of their combined central depressant effects (p. 1064, 1065). "Noteworthy, precautions include prescribing gabapentinoids with opioids due to the combined effects of central nervous system depression." (p. 1065).

**A. Increased neuronal conduction with arousal and disturbed sleep.** Wrong, the stated concern is central depression, not increased neuronal conduction and arousal (p. 1064, 1065).
**B. Reduced opioid effect with development of pharmacologic tolerance.** Wrong, the passage attributes the concern to combined depression rather than reduced opioid effect or tolerance (p. 1064, 1065).
**C. Accelerated opioid clearance with loss of analgesic effect.** Wrong, accelerated opioid clearance is not the mechanism given for this warning; the stated concern is combined central depression (p. 1064, 1065).
**D. Combined depressant effects on the central nervous system.** Correct, this is the explicit reason for caution when gabapentinoids are prescribed with opioids (p. 1064, 1065).

Source: Hazzard's Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8th ed., pp. 1064, 1065.

q: A 74-year-old woman with depression and osteoarthritis has persistent hip pain despite acetaminophen. She takes sertraline and declines NSAIDs because of gastrointestinal concerns. The team is considering a supervised change to duloxetine. Which source-described action explains its potential analgesic role?
o: Inhibition of cyclooxygenase to reduce prostaglandin formation
Modulation of pain pathways through serotonin and norepinephrine
Blockade of voltage-gated calcium channels to reduce excitability
Increased GABA activity to reduce neuronal excitability
explanation:
**Duloxetine**, an SNRI, can be used as a coanalgesic because serotonin and norepinephrine modulate pain pathways. Hazzard describes inhibition of ascending pain pathways and promotion of descending inhibitory pathways; this explains an analgesic role without establishing that it is the safest option for this individual (pp. 1063-1064).
"Modulation of pain pathway via serotonin, norepinephrine" (p. 1063).
"By increasing the activity of serotonin and norepinephrine, these medications modulate the pain pathway to inhibit ascending pain pathways and promote descending pain inhibitory pathways." (p. 1064).

**A. Inhibition of cyclooxygenase to reduce prostaglandin formation.** Wrong, the source assigns cyclooxygenase inhibition to NSAIDs, not to duloxetine (p. 1063).
**B. Modulation of pain pathways through serotonin and norepinephrine.** Correct, this is the SNRI mechanism listed for duloxetine and explained in the text (pp. 1063-1064).
**C. Blockade of voltage-gated calcium channels to reduce excitability.** Wrong, voltage-gated calcium-channel blockade is the mechanism listed for gabapentinoids (p. 1063).
**D. Increased GABA activity to reduce neuronal excitability.** Wrong, increased GABA activity is the mechanism listed for benzodiazepines, not SNRIs (p. 1064).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 1063, 1064.

q: An 84-year-old man with knee osteoarthritis still has pain that limits walking despite topical and oral treatment. Which statement about a local intervention is supported by Hazzard?
o: Hyaluronic acid injections have clear benefit after trial bias is addressed
TNF inhibitor injections are recommended for treating erosive osteoarthritis
Corticosteroid injections provide short-term relief of pain from knee osteoarthritis
Mesenchymal stem cell injections are approved for routine osteoarthritis care
explanation:
**Intra-articular corticosteroids** provide short-term relief of osteoarthritis pain, including persistent knee symptoms. The source distinguishes that symptomatic benefit from unproven durable benefit and from other interventions lacking clear efficacy or remaining experimental (pp. 788–789, 1067). “However, long-term benefits are not well established.” (p. 1067).

**A. Hyaluronic acid injections have clear benefit after trial bias is addressed.** Wrong, the reviewed meta-analyses found no clear symptomatic benefit after addressing bias, which does not support the claimed clear benefit (p. 789).
**B. TNF inhibitor injections are recommended for treating erosive osteoarthritis.** Wrong, TNF inhibitors did not prove efficacious for erosive osteoarthritis and are not recommended for that use (p. 788).
**C. Corticosteroid injections provide short-term relief of pain from knee osteoarthritis.** Correct, knee corticosteroid injections outperform placebo in the short term, matching the proposed relief of persistent osteoarthritis pain (p. 1067).
**D. Mesenchymal stem cell injections are approved for routine osteoarthritis care.** Wrong, the source describes mesenchymal stem cell therapy as experimental and not approved for routine use outside an approved clinical trial (p. 789).

Source: Hazzard’s Geriatric Medicine and Gerontology, 8e, pp. 788–789, 1067.
label: Source: Hazzard 8e (marked) · p. 1067

q: An 81-year-old man with diabetes and peripheral neuropathy has worsening burning foot pain for three months. He takes metformin, lisinopril, and aspirin; HbA1c is 8.2%, and monofilament sensation is absent bilaterally. He lives alone and recently stopped driving because of pain. Gabapentin 300 mg three times daily caused severe dizziness. Which listed analgesic option belongs to the serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitor class?
o: Pregabalin
Duloxetine
Amitriptyline
Capsaicin
explanation:
**Duloxetine** is an SNRI used for neuropathic pain. SNRIs modulate pain pathways through serotonin and norepinephrine; this class identification does not establish that duloxetine is the best next treatment for this individual (pp. 1063–1064).
"Serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (SNRIs)" (p. 1063).
"Duloxetine (Cymbalta)" (p. 1063).

**A. Pregabalin.** Wrong, pregabalin is a gabapentinoid that blocks voltage-gated calcium channels, not an SNRI (p. 1063).
**B. Duloxetine.** Correct, duloxetine is explicitly listed under serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibitors (p. 1063).
**C. Amitriptyline.** Wrong, amitriptyline is a tricyclic antidepressant; overlapping neurotransmitter effects do not make it an SNRI (p. 1063).
**D. Capsaicin.** Wrong, capsaicin acts at TRPV-1 receptors on nociceptors rather than through serotonin-norepinephrine reuptake inhibition (p. 1064).

Source: Hazzard 8e, pp. 1063, 1064.

q: A 77-year-old woman with chronic low-back pain has marked lumbar facet arthropathy on MRI, local facet tenderness, and pain on extension and lateral rotation. She has hypertension and osteoporosis and takes amlodipine, alendronate, and acetaminophen. Physical therapy gave little relief, and tramadol caused nausea. Which description of medial branch blocks agrees with Hazzard?
o: They target nerves supplying the facet joints to provide diagnostic information
They target nerves supplying the facet joints and demonstrate arthropathy severity on imaging
They target the vertebral body and test whether a compression fracture causes pain
They target the sacroiliac joint space and test whether sacroiliac pain is present
explanation:
**Medial branch blocks** address the nerve supply of lumbar facet joints. Hazzard identifies the medial branch nerves of the dorsal primary ramus as their innervation and states: "Facet MB joint diagnostic nerve blocks are most commonly performed due to fair to good evidence regarding efficacy." (p. 1066). The examination findings support evaluating facet-mediated pain, but MRI severity and a diagnostic block answer different questions.

**A. They target nerves supplying the facet joints to provide diagnostic information.** Correct, this links the relevant facet-joint innervation with the diagnostic procedure described by the source (p. 1066).
**B. They target nerves supplying the facet joints and demonstrate arthropathy severity on imaging.** Wrong, imaging characterizes arthropathy severity; a nerve block does not produce that imaging assessment (p. 1066).
**C. They target the vertebral body and test whether a compression fracture causes pain.** Wrong, the facet block targets the medial branch nerve supply, not the vertebral body used in the compression-fracture procedures discussed on this page (p. 1066).
**D. They target the sacroiliac joint space and test whether sacroiliac pain is present.** Wrong, the page describes sacroiliac interventions separately; a lumbar facet medial branch block addresses facet-joint innervation, not an injection into the sacroiliac space (p. 1066).

Source: Hazzard, 8th edition, pp. 1066.
